bib.title: A Sober Look at Clustering Stability

question: What does stability of a clustering algorithm under resampling actually measure, and is it a valid tool for choosing the number of clusters k?
hypothesis: For large samples, stability is determined by whether the clustering objective has a unique minimizer (stable) or symmetric multiple minimizers (unstable), not by whether k is right.
contributions: A formal definition of stability for sample-based clustering algorithms
Theorem: unique risk minimizer implies stability for risk-converging R-minimizing algorithms
Theorem: a symmetry permuting minimizers implies instability
Analogous results for two spectral clustering variants
Examples where stability contradicts the intuitive choice of k

results.claim: If P has a unique risk minimizer, any R-minimizing, risk-converging clustering algorithm is stable on P (Theorem 10); this covers k-means and k-medians.
results.setup: Risk optimization scheme (X,S,P,R); algorithm exactly minimizes empirical risk and converges in probability to opt(P); stability = limsup over m of expected clustering distance between clusterings of two independent samples; asymptotic in sample size.
results.quote: If P has unique minimizer C∗, then any R-minimizing clustering algorithm which is risk converging is stable on P.

results.claim: If the risk is ODD, the distance is ODD, P has n distinct minimizers and a P-preserving symmetry g moves every minimizer (d_P(C*,g(C*))>0), then any R-minimizing risk-convergent algorithm is unstable on P (Theorem 15); the proof gives stab >= r(0.9)^2/(2n^2) where r = min_i d_P(C*_i, g(C*_i)).
results.setup: Same as Theorem 10 plus ODD risk and ODD clustering distance (Hamming and information-based distances are ODD) and a measure-preserving symmetry g.
results.quote: then any R-minimizing clustering algorithm which is risk convergent is unstable on P.

results.claim: Stability does not indicate the right number of clusters: it is set by symmetry of the data distribution, which is independent of k.
results.setup: Center-based (k-means, k-medians) and spectral clustering, large-sample limit.
results.quote: stability does NOT reflect the validity or meaningfulness of the choice of the number of clusters.

results.claim: Uniform distribution on [0,1]: k-means and k-medians have exactly one risk minimizer for every k (equal-width intervals), so both are stable for every k.
results.setup: One-dimensional, Euclidean metric, population-level argument via Theorem 10.
results.quote: both k-medians and k-means have exactly one risk minimizer

results.claim: Uniform on [0,4] U [12,16], k=3: two optimal center triples, (2,13,15) and (1,3,14), related by g(x)=16-x, so k-means and k-medians are unstable. Shifting weight slightly (first interval a little under 1/2) leaves one optimal triple (2,13,15) and they become stable for the same k.
results.setup: Fig 2; population-level argument, k=3, one dimension.
results.quote: both k-means and k-median have exactly two optimal triples of centers (2, 13, 15) and (1, 3, 14).

results.claim: Normalized spectral clustering (Shi-Malik relaxation, then k-means on the embedding) is stable if the limit clustering is unique (Theorem 16); the kernel-k-means relaxation is stable if the kernel-k-means objective has a unique optimizer (Theorem 17). Theorem 16 proof is only a sketch relying on von Luxburg, Belkin, Bousquet 2004.
results.setup: Compact X; similarity s non-negative, symmetric, continuous, bounded away from 0; first k eigenfunctions unique and k-means objective on the embedding has a unique minimizer (Thm 16).

results.claim: Symmetry causes spectral instability: a graph automorphism makes an eigenvalue multiple, so eigenvectors (and clusterings) are ambiguous; the 4-vertex square graph has Laplacian eigenvalues 0,1,1,2 and yields the two symmetric clusterings {x1,x2},{x3,x4} or {x1,x3},{x2,x4}.
results.setup: Sec 6.3, sketch only; finite samples of symmetric data are nearly symmetric, so small perturbations pick the eigenvector.
results.quote: The Laplacian L of this graph has the eigenvalues 0, 1, 1, 2

results.claim: Constant clusterings (e.g. one cluster) are trivially stable on any distribution, so stability alone says nothing about quality.
results.quote: is stable on any probability distribution P.

results.claim: Conjecture 11 (unproved): multiple minimizers imply instability for any R-minimizing, risk-converging algorithm; only the stronger symmetry condition is proved.
results.setup: Euclidean space; authors know no counterexample.
results.quote: While we cannot, at this stage, prove the above conjecture in the generality,

limits: Asymptotic only: concerns stab(A,P)=limsup over m; finite-sample/variance instability is set aside ('we mainly focus on the first kind of stability').

Assumes the algorithm exactly minimizes the empirical risk (R-minimizing) and is risk converging; k-means local minima / non-exact optimization is not covered by the theorems (mentioned as a similar effect that diminishes with sample size).
Conjecture 11 (multiple minimizers imply instability) is unproved; only symmetry is proved.
Theorem 16 proof is a sketch; spectral symmetry argument in 6.3 is also a sketch.
No experiments on real data; support is theorems and hand-built examples. The claim that most real data are not perfectly symmetric is a belief ('we believe').
Authors leave open what features of real data make stability work in practice, and concede success of stability for choosing k 'should be viewed as an exception rather than the rule'.
Only center-based and spectral clustering are covered; other paradigms left open.
Authors say results do not contradict supervised-learning stability results.

terms.definition: stab(A,P,m) = E over S1,S2 ~ P^m of d_P(A(S1),A(S2)); stab(A,P) = limsup_m stab(A,P,m); A is stable for P if stab(A,P)=0.
For every eps>0 and delta in (0,1) there is m0 such that for m>m0, Pr[R(P,A(S)) < opt(P)+eps] > 1-delta for any P.
For all eta>0 there is eps>0 with R(P,C) < opt(P)+eps implying d_P(C*,C) < eta.
Depends only on distances and distribution: invariant under every P-preserving symmetry g.

code.snippet: stab(A, P, m) = E_{S1~P^m, S2~P^m} d_P(A(S1), A(S2));  stab(A,P) = limsup_{m->inf} stab(A,P,m)
